title: Ibn Kathir
hook: a commentary explaining the Qur'an by the Qur'an and hadith
tomorrow: a verse about washing your hands. where's the law in it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Tabari kept all the voices on the page, then judged. Today, a commentator with a rule for where to look first.
screen: `ALL THE VOICES.` → `TODAY, WHERE TO LOOK FIRST.`

segments.voice: A friend drops a word in the group chat you don't understand. Before you ask, you scroll up, and there it is: she explained it a few messages back. Ibn Kathir, a scholar of Damascus, opens his commentary with that same rule. The best way to explain the Qur'an is by the Qur'an: what one place says briefly, another spells out. If that isn't enough, go to the Sunna, the Prophet's own teaching. Then to his companions, then to their students. The book explains itself, first.
screen: `SCROLL UP: SHE ALREADY SAID IT.` → `QUR'AN BY QUR'AN.` → `THEN SUNNA, THEN COMPANIONS.`

segments.voice: Watch him do it with the verse of the Throne, Ayat al-Kursi. It opens: "Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal." Ibn Kathir notes those same words open another surah, Al Imran, so one passage lights the other. Then a hadith: the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, asked his companion Ubayy ibn Ka'b which verse of the book is greatest. Ubayy said this one, and the Prophet struck him on the chest and said, may knowledge delight you. Now the debate inside the tradition. One side, Ibn Kathir's: start with the Qur'an and the reports, because reasoning alone can read yourself into the text. He cites a hadith warning against speaking about the Qur'an by mere opinion. The other side, commentators who give reason a bigger room: the Qur'an itself asks people to ponder it, and reports don't answer every question a new age asks. Reason, carefully used, is part of obeying the book. Notice how much they share. Both begin with the Qur'an. Both use reports and reasoning. They differ on which leads, and how far reasoning may go.
screen: `THE SAME WORDS OPEN AL IMRAN.` · `UBAYY: THE GREATEST VERSE.` · `VIEW ONE: REPORTS LEAD.` · `VIEW TWO: REASON, CAREFULLY.` · then, large: `THE BOOK EXPLAINS ITSELF.`

segments.voice: If you know Ayat al-Kursi in Arabic, say it softly, once, slowly. If not, say its opening in English, one phrase per breath: Allah, there is no God save him, the Alive, the Eternal. Let each phrase finish before the next begins.
screen: `THE VERSE OF THE THRONE.` · `ONE PHRASE PER BREATH.`

segments.voice: Ibn Kathir: a scholar of Damascus whose commentary explains the Qur'an by the Qur'an first, then by the Prophet's teaching and his companions.
The line today: the book explains itself, so scroll up before you guess. Commentators, two of six.

howItsDone: Ibn Kathir's tafsir is read in mosques, study circles and homes, in Arabic and in translation; hadith encourage reciting Ayat al-Kursi after the daily prayers and before sleep.

fork.setup: your study circle splits: one friend says stick to the transmitted reports; another says reason has a big role. you're asked to give the reports side's best case. what is it?
options: reasoning is forbidden in Islam, so thinking about verses is wrong.
old reports are simpler, so they're easier for everyone to follow.
reason alone can read you into the text; reports keep you close to it.
fork.reveal: that's Ibn Kathir's worry, and the other side's best case is just as real: the Qur'an asks people to ponder it, and new questions need careful reason.

original.note: Arabic: the verse of the Throne (Qur'an 2:255).

trapdoor: what you thought: a commentator tells you what he thinks a verse means.
what it means: Ibn Kathir explains the Qur'an by the Qur'an first, then the Prophet's teaching, then the companions and their students.
what a scholar hears: the method in his preface (following Ibn Taymiyya), tafsir by transmission (bil-ma'thur), and the debate over the place of reasoned opinion (ra'y).

options: Start where Ibn Kathir does: the Qur'an's other verses and the hadith, before anyone's theory.
If the guy's reasoning sounds smart, it's as good as any classical commentary.
Tell Jordan only scholars may read it, so it's really not for him.
chat.meaning: Ibn Kathir explains the Qur'an by the Qur'an first, then the Prophet's teaching, so the book speaks before any outside theory.

Ibn Kathir.meaning: a scholar of Damascus who wrote a Qur'an commentary

Ayat al-Kursi.meaning: the verse of the Throne, Qur'an 2:255

Ubayy ibn Ka'b.meaning: a companion of the Prophet, known as a Qur'an reciter

sources.quoted: Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal.

sources.ref: Qur'an 3:2 (the same words open Al Imran)
Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Qur'an al-'Azim, preface (the best way of tafsir: Qur'an by Qur'an, then Sunna, then the companions, then the successors) and his note on 2:255
Sahih Muslim 810 (Ubayy ibn Ka'b and the greatest verse)
Jami' al-Tirmidhi 2950-2951 (warning against speaking about the Qur'an by opinion, without knowledge); Qur'an 4:82 (will they not ponder the Qur'an?)

notes: Pickthall 2:255 opening as used on earlier days; confirm wording.
Ibn Kathir's preface method (taken from Ibn Taymiyya's Muqaddima fi Usul al-Tafsir) summarized; confirm. That he links 2:255 to 3:2 and cites Muslim 810 in his note on Ayat al-Kursi: confirm.

Debate: tafsir bil-ma'thur vs. a larger role for ra'y (e.g. al-Razi); no names given for the second side. Tirmidhi numbers for the warning hadith (graded differently by scholars); Qur'an 4:82 paraphrased. Confirm both views are fairly stated.
howItsDone: reciting Ayat al-Kursi after prayers and before sleep is based on hadith (al-Nasa'i; al-Bukhari 2311); descriptive. Confirm.
